title: NAT-Egress-and-Private-DNS-Playbook-Notes
content:
Purpose:
This is a working playbook for private (VPC / on-prem) deployments focused on networking primitives that commonly cause outages or security issues: private DNS (split-horizon), ingress/egress design, NAT strategy, firewall rules, and Kubernetes network policies. It contains Terraform module notes, operational upgrade steps, and a checklist for preflight validation.

Scope & assumptions:
- Target environments: cloud VPCs (AWS/GCP/Azure) and typical on-prem rack + edge NAT/egress appliances.
- We assume the control plane (Redwood Private) is either customer-managed or our light control-plane that peers with customer VPCs.
- Kubernetes clusters are CNI-enabled (Calico or Cilium recommended).
- Customers expect no public IPs for model-serving nodes; egress must be tightly controlled.

High-level recommendations (summary):
1) Private DNS: use provider private zones for split-horizon for internal service discovery; run CoreDNS as a customer-managed add-on in clusters with conditional forwarding for infra zones.
2) Egress: prefer a small set of centralized egress NAT gateways (cloud NAT, NAT gateway, or on-prem NAT appliance) and an egress proxy for auditing and TLS inspection where required.
3) Ingress: terminate TLS at an ingress controller inside the VPC (Envoy/Contour/NGINX) and avoid opening node ports; use internal load balancers.
4) Firewall rules: whitelist-heavy approach, explicit ephemeral ports for kubelet/healthchecks, and keep a standardized set of managed rules in Terraform modules.
5) NetworkPolicy: require default-deny at namespace level; provide app-level allow lists for control plane traffic.

Topology sketches (ASCII):
Cloud VPC example:
  Internet -> ALB (internet-facing) -> internal ALB -> Envoy ILB -> pod
  OR (private-only)
  On-prem site -> VPN/Transit -> VPC (Private LB / ILB) -> Envoy -> pods

Private DNS patterns:
- AWS: Route53 private hosted zones per account/region. Use conditional forwarding from CoreDNS (in EKS) to the Route53 resolver for cross-VPC resolution.
- GCP: use Cloud DNS private zones + DNS peering. For on-prem we recommend running a local authoritative resolver for local zones and forwarding unknown queries upstream.
- Split-horizon: maintain two zone views: public (for normal internet names) and internal (for internal hostnames like *.svc.redwood.local). Do NOT leak internal records to public.
- CoreDNS notes: add "hosts" plugin for static shortnames (for bootstrap), and "forward" to send unresolved queries to the VPC resolver. Example Corefile fragment:

  .:53 {
    errors
    health
    ready
    hosts /etc/coredns/hosts {
      fallthrough
    }
    forward . 169.254.169.253 {
      max_concurrent 1000
    }
    cache 30
  }

NAT / egress strategy details:
- Cloud: prefer managed NAT (Cloud NAT / AWS NAT Gateway) for simplicity and scaling. Allocate small number of egress IPs maintained in Terraform for ACL whitelisting by partners.
- On-prem: single/high-availability pair of NAT appliances or use source-NAT on edge routers.
- Egress proxy: add an HTTP(S) proxy (squid / envoy) in front of NAT for outbound policy, logging, and corporate filtering. Point pod egress to proxy via IP tables or sidecar where required.
- IP exhaustion mitigation: when scaling many clusters, use multiple NAT pools and per-cluster SNAT mapping; avoid single /32 egress IP.

Firewall rules and security groups (recommended minimal set):
- Control plane -> kube API: allow from jump hosts / management subnets only.
- Node -> registry/storage: allow outbound 443 to artifact registries (list in Terraform var).
- Health checks: allow LB health check ranges (document cloud provider ranges).
- Inter-node: allow VXLAN/overlay ports (Calico IP-in-IP / WireGuard) and BGP if used.
- Egress: default deny, allow explicit ranges: DNS(53), NTP(123), proxy(3128/443), cloud metadata only for managed agents.

Terraform module notes (observations from PRs and in-field ops):
- Module: redwood/vpc-network (inputs):
  - variable cluster_cidrs (list of CIDRs) -> string list
  - variable nat_mode (string) -> ["managed_nat","egress_proxy","none"]
  - variable private_dns_zones (map) -> map of zone name -> cidrs (store as json string in TF state to keep flat)
  - variable allowed_egress_destinations (list) -> list of CIDR or hostnames (we recommend canonicalizing to IPs via preflight)
  - output egress_ip_addresses (list)

- Practical guidance: keep module idempotent for NAT replacements: create new NAT gateway resources with new IPs, update route table to point to new gateway, then decommission old NAT only after connections drain. Avoid in-place replacement of NAT when possible.

- Example HCL (text snippet for docs):

  module "redwood_vpc" {
    source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules.git//vpc?ref=main"

    cluster_cidrs = ["10.10.0.0/16"]
    nat_mode = "managed_nat"
    private_dns_zones = jsonencode({"redwood.local" = ["10.10.0.0/16"]})
    allowed_egress_destinations = ["13.32.0.0/15", "52.95.0.0/16"]
  }

Upgrade plan (NAT or DNS changes) - recommended runbook:
1) Preflight:
  - Validate current state: list active NAT IPs, active connections, firewall rules.
  - Create a temporary "canary" cluster in the same VPC to exercise DNS and egress paths.
  - Confirm logging/metrics for egress request rates (so we can spot regressions).
  - Make sure backups of CoreDNS config and zone files exist (S3/GCS).
2) Apply Terraform in non-destructive mode against a staging project: plan -> review with on-call network engineer.
3) Create new NAT gateway (or configure managed NAT) with new IPs.
4) Update route tables to point to the new gateway for a subset of subnets (canary rollout).
5) Monitor for 15-30 minutes for connection errors, DNS failures, application errors (403/502).
6) If stable, progressively update remaining subnets in waves.
7) Decommission old NAT after 24–72 hours of stability.
8) Post-change: update documentation, Terraform state, and notify partners for IP allowlist changes.

Rollback triggers: sudden spike in 5xx errors, DNS resolution failures for internal names, or partner complaining about blocked egress. Rollback is to re-point the changed route table entries back to old gateway immediately, plus open a P1 channel.

On-prem specifics and edgecases:
- When clusters are behind NAT appliances that do not support hairpin NAT, use egress proxy to prevent loopbacks.
- BGP advertisement: prefer not to rely on dynamic BGP for ephemeral egress pools; keep a small, stable range for partner whitelisting.
- VLAN segmentation: clearly map tenant namespaces to VLANs and ensure firewall rules apply at edge leaf switches as part of Terraform-managed config if possible.

Kubernetes NetworkPolicy and CNI recommendations:
- Default namespace policy: "deny all ingress/egress". Provide a standard policy template for Redwood control-plane traffic:
  - allow egress to control-plane IPs and ports (443, 8443).
  - allow DNS to cluster DNS service (cluster-ip:53).
  - allow kubelet health probes between nodes.
- Calico: use GlobalNetworkPolicy for infra-wide rules, and NamespaceNetworkPolicy for per-customer isolation. Tag workloads via labels (role=redwood-agent). Example Calico GlobalNetworkPolicy snippet (as text):

  apiVersion: projectcalico.org/v3
  kind: GlobalNetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: redwood-controlplane-egress
  spec:
    selector: role == 'redwood-agent'
    order: 100
    egress:
      - action: Allow
        protocol: TCP
        destination:
          nets: ["10.0.0.0/8"]
    types: [Egress]

Operational checks and observability:
- DNS: query local CoreDNS from a debug pod and the VPC resolver to compare answers. Record timestamps.
- Egress: run a synthetic test that hits partner IP allowlists (to confirm NAT mapping).
- Firewall: attempt a port-scan from a privileged debug host inside a tenant subnet to ensure only expected ports are open.
- Logging: egress proxy logs + VPC flow logs should be ingested into an analytics pipeline for quick post-change debugging.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Should we standardize on Envoy as the default egress proxy for TLS termination / observability? (Dev + Security to decide)
- How to encode private_dns_zones in TF variables without using nested maps (proposal: jsonencode string, add helper scripts to validate zone content).
- Add an automated preflight tool that resolves all hostnames in allowed_egress_destinations and converts to IPs; PR tracked at INFRA-2381.

Runbook checklist (short):
- [ ] Confirm backups of DNS zones
- [ ] Create canary cluster / canary subnets
- [ ] Apply new NAT in staging and smoke-test
- [ ] Update route tables gradually
- [ ] Monitor metrics (dns_errors, egress_5xx, flow_logs anomalies)
- [ ] Decommission old resources after stability

Appendix: quick grep-friendly snippets
- Identify NAT gateways: aws ec2 describe-nat-gateways --filters "Name=vpc-id,Values=${VPC}"
- Check CoreDNS logs: kubectl -n kube-system logs -l k8s-app=coredns
- Egress IP mapping (GCP): gcloud compute addresses list --filter="labels=egress"

Notes-to-self:
- Keep examples provider-agnostic in doc but include provider-specific subsections for common pitfalls.
- Share with security / platform next week for comments.
- Follow up: add kube-proxy iptables vs ipvs note and impact on overlay MTU.

End of draft.
